10.text: Quick check. A scene explains the word label, next to the walkthrough's table. After step one, where does the word go?

11.text: You decided which scenes show the real thing: the brief picks, decision D-166. This video's brief names its own, like the map and the check's lines; the rest explain with pictures, and nothing warns.

12.text: Step two writes a motion language: which move means what. A camera, the view that moves over one picture, pushes in to a detail and pulls back, like this. A cut starts a chapter or a quick check; a push, the next scene; a fade, the same place later.

13.text: The checks keep the answer safe. Nothing the camera moves may reach the answer bar at the bottom. And the frame check fails a question scene whose camera is not at rest when it ends, so the cards stay whole and still where you click.

14.text: Quick check. A quick check's cards sit inside a camera that is still zoomed in when the scene ends. What does the frame check do?

15.text: Step three, which you decided: the page keeps today's look, made readable, decision D-167. It is already built. Its fonts ship with the page, and its words sit in three solid shades on a real scale of sizes. And the accent colour, the one colour for what waits on you, is the darker coral, decision D-142, in the videos too.

16.text: Quick check. After step three, someone opens the review page on a computer without Inter, one of its fonts. What do they see?

17.text: Step four: no mass rebuild. A video takes the new style when a review asks for changes, only in the scenes it touches. The system video is rebuilt once, whole, since every new viewer starts there. This video is the first made this way.

18.text: Quick check. A review of the fewer-stops plan video asks for changes to its step two only. After this plan, which of its scenes take the new style?

19.text: That is the plan: four steps, and both questions decided. The brief picks which scenes show the real thing, and the page keeps today's look, made readable. Draw on any step to leave a note, or approve.

01.text: Here are twelve scenes from our videos. A scene is one picture and a sentence or two of voice. Each is built the same way: a small heading, step ticks, a few thin boxes. In a hundred and eleven scenes, things pop in six hundred times, and almost every cut is one fade.

02.text: This is the review page's Terms panel today. It names three fonts and ships none of them, so each viewer sees whatever their computer has. Its words sit in five shades of grey.

03.text: The plan's answer starts with the real thing: the actual file, table, command output or screen a scene is about, shown just as it is, instead of a box of words describing it. Here is a scene from the fewer-stops walkthrough today: boxes of words about its table. And the same scene showing the real thing: the table itself, from its file.

04.text: But the real thing is never every file. Say a change touches ten files, like this real one from our repo, the terms check: nine files. The scene shows its map first: each file, with one plain line on what changed there. One of them carries the idea: the check itself.

05.text: So the scene opens that one file, at the lines that carry the idea. Here the check finds where a word is first said, and where it is explained. Said before it is explained, it warns. The other eight files stay a line on the map.

06.text: And where the code is hard to read, a picture explains it better. Say the word label is said in scene two and explained in scene four: the check warns about scene two. The real thing is there to make the change clear, not for its own sake.

07.text: So the plan makes three changes. Steps one and two: scenes show the real thing, with checks that keep the answer safe. Step three keeps the page's look, its type, colours and shapes, and makes it easy to read. Step four says when old videos change.

08.text: Four earlier decisions still hold. The screen says plain words. You answer on the frame's own cards. Each step gets a quick check. And the system video is kept current after each build.

09.text: Step one makes showing the real thing the rule. Before, a scene about a code change drew cards about it; now it shows the change itself. And a pinned word replaces the card: a plain word placed on the thing it names. Before, label had a card; now it sits on the table's label column.
